title: try/catch with unknown and type-safe error handling
hook: In JavaScript, anything can be thrown — a string, a number, a plain object. TypeScript types the catch variable as unknown so you must narrow before using it. That honesty at API boundaries prevents silent bugs in production workers.

blocks.text: Since TypeScript 4.0, the default type of a **catch** variable is **unknown**, not **any**. **unknown** means "we do not know what was thrown" — you cannot read `.message`, call methods, or pass it to a function until you **narrow** it with `instanceof Error`, a type guard, or an explicit check. This matches JavaScript reality: `throw "oops"` and `throw { code: 404 }` are legal. C# is stricter — only `System.Exception`-derived types compile — but TypeScript runs on JavaScript, so the type system admits the truth at the boundary.

entries.plainDefinition: A top type that is safe — you must narrow before use. Unlike any, unknown cannot be assigned or accessed without checks.
entries.example: catch (e: unknown) { if (e instanceof Error) console.log(e.message); }

entries.plainDefinition: Refining a broad type to a specific one using control flow — instanceof, typeof, in, or custom guards.
Runtime test that the thrown value is an Error (or subclass). The most common first guard in catch blocks.
tsconfig flag (default true in strict) that types catch variables as unknown instead of any.

blocks.text: A fetch wrapper, queue consumer, or Express error middleware receives failures from libraries you do not control. Assuming `catch (e: Error)` is a lie — a dependency might throw a string or a rejected promise with a plain object. Treating unknown as Error and reading `.message` without a check causes runtime crashes in the handler that was supposed to recover. At FAANG-level interviews, "catch is unknown, narrow first" separates engineers who understand JavaScript semantics from those who only know syntax.

blocks.title: Catch is an API boundary
blocks.body: Every catch block is a boundary between untyped throw sites and your typed application code. Narrow before logging, mapping to HTTP status codes, or rethrowing. Never cast with `as Error` without a runtime check.

sections.heading: How to narrow safely at the boundary

items.title: Catch as unknown
items.body: Let TypeScript default to unknown (or annotate explicitly). Do not opt back into any.

items.title: Check instanceof Error
items.body: Most thrown values in well-behaved code are Error instances. Use message and stack safely after this check.

items.title: Handle non-Error throws
items.body: Strings, numbers, and plain objects need explicit branches — stringify or map to a domain error.

items.title: Normalize and rethrow or return Result
items.body: Convert to a consistent shape (AppError, Result failure) before crossing service layers.

diagram.title: Narrowing unknown at a catch boundary
diagram.source:
flowchart TD
  THROW[Any value thrown] --> CATCH[catch e: unknown]
  CATCH --> INST{e instanceof Error?}
  INST -->|yes| ERR[Use e.message / e.stack]
  INST -->|no| STR{typeof e === string?}
  STR -->|yes| MSG[Wrap as Error or log string]
  STR -->|no| OBJ[JSON.stringify or domain mapper]
  ERR --> NORMALIZE[Normalize to AppError or Result]
  MSG --> NORMALIZE
  OBJ --> NORMALIZE

snippet.label: Default unknown catch — the honest baseline
snippet.explanation: Line 7: catch types e as unknown. Lines 8–10: instanceof Error narrows to Error so .message is legal. Lines 11–12: non-Error throws (string, object) get String(e) — no unsafe cast.

snippet.label: Reusable toError helper
snippet.explanation: Lines 1–8: one place to normalize any thrown value to Error. Line 14: after toError, logging and rethrow use a consistent type. Keeps catch blocks thin in workers and middleware.

snippet.label: Why catch (e: any) is a regression
snippet.explanation: Line 3: any lets you access .message without proof — runtime undefined if e is a string. Lines 8–12: unknown forces the instanceof check before property access.

blocks.title: Casting unknown to Error without a check
blocks.body: const err = e as Error is a lie at compile time and a crash at runtime when a library throws "ECONNRESET". Always narrow with instanceof or a helper like toError.

blocks.title: Empty catch blocks
blocks.body: catch (e: unknown) { } swallows poison messages in queue workers. Log, map to Result, retry transient faults, or rethrow — never succeed silently.

blocks.text: unknown at catch boundaries is TypeScript admitting JavaScript semantics — unlike C# where throw is typed. In production, measure non-Error throw rate from third-party packages; axios and node-fetch usually reject with Error but legacy callbacks may throw strings. useUnknownInCatchVariables should stay true in strict configs. At service boundaries, normalize once with toError or map to Result — do not scatter instanceof checks. Promise rejections follow the same rule: .catch((e: unknown) => ...). For async middleware, wrap the entire handler and normalize at the outer edge so inner code can assume AppError.

snippet.label: Failure mode — non-Error throw crashes naive handler
snippet.explanation: Lines 3–4: string throw is valid JavaScript. Line 12: any hides the bug — e.message is undefined. Lines 20–22: unknown + toError produces a reliable message for metrics and alerts.

blocks.title: What gets you rejected in interviews
blocks.body: Saying catch (e: Error) is safe without instanceof. Using as Error to silence the compiler. Not knowing useUnknownInCatchVariables exists. Claiming TypeScript can catch only TypeError like C# catches IOException.

interviewTakeaways: catch defaults to unknown in strict TypeScript — anything can be thrown at runtime.
Narrow with instanceof Error or a toError helper before reading .message or .stack.
Never use as Error without a runtime check — that is how handlers crash while handling errors.
60s: unknown in catch is honest JS semantics. instanceof or toError at boundaries. No typed catch like C#. Result for expected failures, throw for exceptional.
Follow-up: how do you handle non-Error throws from a legacy npm package?
commonPitfalls: catch (e: any) or as Error without instanceof — compiles but crashes on string throws.
Empty catch blocks in workers — poison messages or silent data loss.
Strong answer: 'unknown default, toError at boundary, metrics on normalized message, never cast without check.'

jsTsCorrelations.note: JavaScript allows throw "text" or throw 42. TypeScript unknown in catch reflects this — there is no compile-time throw type.
C# catch (IOException ex) is enforced by the compiler. TypeScript cannot filter catch by type — you inspect inside the block after narrowing unknown.
